[Chapter 2](02AdditiveModel.qmd) sorted the parts of a ring two ways: by who shares them, and by how fast they change. The tool for the second sort is a filter. It splits a series into a slow part and a fast part, and nearly every method in the book uses one. This aside starts with the simplest filter there is, then takes up the one dendrochronology leans on hardest, the smoothing spline, and ends with the ways the field's spline looks a little odd to someone from statistics or signal processing.

```{r}
#| label: flt-setup
#| message: false
library(dplR)
library(ggplot2)
source("R/sim-collection.R")
```

`ggplot2` draws the figures. The simulated collection comes from the book's `R/` folder, and [The Simulated Collection](03SimulatedCollection.qmd) describes it.

## A Filter Sorts by Speed

Here is a made-up series with a known answer: a slow wave that takes 50 years to go up and down, plus a new random number every year.

```{r}
#| label: flt-made-up
set.seed(2)
years <- 1:100
slow <- sin(2 * pi * years / 50)   # one cycle every 50 years
fast <- rnorm(100, sd = 0.5)       # a new value every year
madeUp <- slow + fast
```

The simplest filter is a running mean. Replace each year with the average of itself and its neighbors. With a window of three years, year 2 becomes the mean of years 1, 2 and 3, and you can check that by hand.

```{r}
#| label: flt-by-hand
# stats::filter with three equal weights of 1/3 is a three-year running mean.
# Each year is averaged with the year before and the year after.
smooth3 <- as.numeric(stats::filter(madeUp, rep(1 / 3, 3)))
round(madeUp[1:3], 3)
mean(madeUp[1:3])
smooth3[2]
```

The first and last years have no neighbor on one side, so they come out `NA`. A three-year mean doesn't smooth much. Widen the window to eleven years and the result starts to look like the slow wave.

```{r}
#| label: flt-sides
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "A slow wave plus yearly noise, split by an 11-year running mean. Top: the series (gray), the true slow wave (dashed) and the running mean (solid). Bottom: what the running mean left behind (solid) and the true noise (gray)."
smooth11 <- as.numeric(stats::filter(madeUp, rep(1 / 11, 11)))
left11 <- madeUp - smooth11   # whatever the smooth didn't take

# Two panels, so stack them into one long table with a column saying which
sides <- data.frame(
  year = rep(years, 2),
  data = c(madeUp, fast),
  truth = c(slow, fast),
  filtered = c(smooth11, left11),
  side = rep(c("Slow side (low-pass)", "Fast side (high-pass)"), each = 100)
)
sides$side <- factor(sides$side, levels = unique(sides$side))

ggplot(sides, aes(x = year)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = data), colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(aes(y = truth), linetype = "dashed",
            data = sides[sides$side == "Slow side (low-pass)", ]) +
  geom_line(aes(y = filtered), na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~side, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: flt-sides-values
#| include: false
rSlow <- cor(smooth11, slow, use = "complete.obs")
rFast <- cor(left11, fast, use = "complete.obs")
```

The running mean follows the slow wave at a correlation of `r round(rSlow, 2)`, and what it leaves behind follows the noise at `r round(rFast, 2)`. That is what a filter does. The smooth is the low-pass side, because it lets slow changes through. What's left is the high-pass side. The two add back up to the series, so one filter gives you both, and which side you keep depends on what you are after.

The window decides where the split falls. A three-year mean barely touches anything slower than a few years. An eleven-year mean holds back most of what changes from one year to the next. Every filter in the book has some setting like that, and many arguments about tree-ring methods turn out to be about where it should go.

The running mean is the easiest filter to explain and one of the worst to use. [Smoothing and Filtering](14SmoothingFiltering.qmd) shows it turning some cycles upside down. It's here because you can check it by hand.

## Filtering Is Everywhere in Dendro

Nearly every step from cores to a chronology filters something. A partial list, with where the book takes each up:

- Crossdating keeps the fast side. The crossdating functions divide each series by a 32-year spline and then prewhiten it, which takes out the memory from one year to the next, and prewhitening is a filter too ([Crossdating](06Crossdating.qmd), [Crossdating Statistics](08xAsideCrossdatingStats.qmd)).
- Detrending divides each series by a slow curve and keeps the rest ([Detrending](09Detrending.qmd)). How much slow climate goes out with the curve is the segment-length curse, and it is a question about a filter.
- Regional curve standardization smooths a mean curve by ring age ([Regional Curves](12RegionalCurves.qmd)), and signal-free detrending fits a spline over and over ([Signal-Free](13SignalFree.qmd)).
- Running means, Hanning windows and Butterworth filters are for looking at a finished chronology and splitting it into bands ([Smoothing and Filtering](14SmoothingFiltering.qmd)).

So the spline below is the first of many filters you'll meet, and the one the field uses most.

## The Spline

A cubic smoothing spline is a curve that follows the data but pays a penalty for bending. A stiff spline bends little and follows only the slowest changes. A flexible one bends a lot and chases the data. Cook and Peters brought it into tree-ring work in 1981 for trees in closed forests, where competition pushes growth up and down in ways no fixed growth curve follows [@Cook1981]. In `dplR` the spline is `caps`, for Cook and Peters spline.

Here it is at three stiffnesses on a crowded tree from the simulated collection, where the true age trend is known.

```{r}
#| label: flt-caps
#| fig-cap: "Ring widths of SIM06A, a crowded tree in the simulated collection (gray), its true age trend (thick line), and three splines. The 10-year spline chases the yearly wiggles. The stiffest one, at 67% of the core's length, follows only the broadest shape."
sim <- sim.collection(seed = 1)
width <- sim$truth$rwl$SIM06A
ok <- !is.na(width)                       # the years this core has rings
coreYears <- as.numeric(rownames(sim$truth$rwl))[ok]
coreWidth <- width[ok]
stiffNyrs <- floor(0.67 * length(coreWidth))   # detrend's default stiffness

splines <- data.frame(
  year = rep(coreYears, 3),
  curve = c(caps(coreWidth, nyrs = 10), caps(coreWidth, nyrs = 32),
            caps(coreWidth, nyrs = stiffNyrs)),
  stiffness = rep(c("10 years", "32 years", paste(stiffNyrs, "years")),
                  each = length(coreWidth))
)
splines$stiffness <- factor(splines$stiffness,
                            levels = unique(splines$stiffness))

ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(x = coreYears, y = coreWidth), colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(aes(x = coreYears, y = sim$truth$age$SIM06A[ok]),
            linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_line(data = splines, aes(x = year, y = curve, linetype = stiffness)) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Ring width (mm)", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

None of the three is right. The age trend of a crowded tree has bumps from its neighbors, and each spline is a guess at which wiggles belong to the trend. The stiffness is the guess.

## Setting the Stiffness

How do you say how stiff? In `caps` you name a cycle length, `nyrs`, and a share, `f`, which is 0.5 unless you change it. The spline is made exactly stiff enough that a cycle `nyrs` years long comes through at that share of its size. That is what "a 32-year spline" means in the tree-ring literature [@Cook1990, p. 110-111].

You can check that the way the book checks most things. Make cycles of known length, pass them through a 32-year spline, and see how big they are coming out.

```{r}
#| label: flt-pass
# Pass a cycle of `period` years through a spline and return the share of
# its amplitude that comes out. It is measured away from the ends of the
# series, for a reason that comes up below.
passThrough <- function(period, nyrs = 32, n = 1000) {
  wave <- cos(2 * pi * (1:n) / period)
  smoothed <- caps(wave, nyrs = nyrs)
  middle <- 200:800
  sd(smoothed[middle]) / sd(wave[middle])
}
periods <- c(10, 20, 32, 64, 100)
round(sapply(periods, passThrough), 3)
```

A 32-year cycle comes through at half its size. Faster cycles are almost gone and slower ones come through nearly whole. Cook and Peters worked out the spline's response as a formula [@Cook1990, p. 111]:

$$u(f) = 1 - \frac{1}{1 + p\,\dfrac{\cos 2\pi f + 2}{6(\cos 2\pi f - 1)^2}}$$

where $f$ is frequency, one over the cycle length, and $p$ sets the stiffness. You don't choose $p$. You choose `nyrs` and `f`, and $p$ follows. `splineResponse` does that algebra and then gives the response at any cycle length.

```{r}
#| label: flt-response
#| fig-cap: "The response of a 32-year spline: the share of a cycle's amplitude that the spline curve keeps, by cycle length. The line is the Cook and Peters formula and the points are the cycles passed through caps. The dotted lines mark half the amplitude at 32 years."
# The Cook and Peters (1981) response of a spline that keeps the share `f`
# of a cycle of `nyrs` years
splineResponse <- function(period, nyrs, f = 0.5) {
  # solve u(1 / nyrs) = f for the stiffness p
  w0 <- 2 * pi / nyrs
  p <- (f / (1 - f)) * 6 * (cos(w0) - 1)^2 / (cos(w0) + 2)
  # then the response at every period
  w <- 2 * pi / period
  1 - 1 / (1 + p * (cos(w) + 2) / (6 * (cos(w) - 1)^2))
}

curvePeriods <- 4:150
ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(x = curvePeriods, y = splineResponse(curvePeriods, 32))) +
  geom_point(aes(x = periods, y = sapply(periods, passThrough)), size = 2.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 32, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = "Cycle length (years)", y = "Share of amplitude kept") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: flt-response-values
#| include: false
formulaGap <- max(abs(sapply(periods, passThrough) -
                        splineResponse(periods, 32)))
halfVar <- passThrough(32)^2
```

The points sit on the line. They agree with the formula to `r floor(-log10(formulaGap))` decimal places, so `caps` does what the formula says.

One thing trips people up. The share is of the amplitude, the size of the swing. Variance goes with the square of the amplitude, so half the amplitude is `r round(halfVar, 2)` of the variance. A 32-year spline keeps a quarter of the variance of a 32-year cycle, and you'll often see that described as half.

## Two Defaults, Two Sides

`dplR` uses this spline in two places with very different settings, and they keep opposite sides.

The crossdating functions, `xdate.report` among them, divide each series by a spline with `nyrs = 32` and keep what's left. They want the fast side, the year-to-year wiggles that pin a ring to its year, and a flexible spline takes out the slow changes that would otherwise swamp the comparison. How stiff a spline works best for dating is a question [Crossdating Statistics](08xAsideCrossdatingStats.qmd) tests directly.

`detrend` with `method = "Spline"` sets `nyrs` to 67% of each series' length, the rule Cook gives in the Cook Book [@Cook1990, p. 114]. *Methods of Dendrochronology*, the edited volume everyone calls the Cook Book, is where most of the field's standardization rules were written down. Here the spline curve is the estimate of the age trend, the slow side, and the index is what's left.

```{r}
#| label: flt-defaults
#| include: false
coreLength <- 300
detrendNyrs <- floor(0.67 * coreLength)
# the share of a swing's amplitude left in the index, by swing length
indexKeeps <- function(period) round(100 * (1 - splineResponse(period, detrendNyrs)))
```

So what does a 67% spline leave in the index? In a core `r coreLength` rings long, the spline is set at `r detrendNyrs` years. The index keeps about `r indexKeeps(100)`% of the amplitude of a 100-year swing in climate, `r indexKeeps(200)`% of a 200-year swing and `r indexKeeps(300)`% of a 300-year one. The rest goes out with the curve. That is the segment-length curse, and [Detrending](09Detrending.qmd) takes it up.

## A Little Odd

The spline the field uses is a sensible tool with a long history. It is also a little unusual, and if you move between dendrochronology and statistics or signal processing, it helps to know where.

The first difference is who picks the stiffness. In statistics a smoothing spline's stiffness is usually chosen from the data, by cross-validation or generalized cross-validation. R's own `smooth.spline` does generalized cross-validation unless you tell it otherwise. Dendrochronology fixes the stiffness in advance from a cycle length. That is a filter designer's specification put on a statistician's smoother, and it works because you usually know what cycle lengths you care about better than the data do.

The second is where the cutoff sits. In signal processing a filter's cutoff is usually the half-power point, where the amplitude is $1/\sqrt{2}$, about 0.71. The dendro spline's named length is where the amplitude is half.

```{r}
#| label: flt-half-power
# The cycle length at which a 32-year spline keeps 71% of the amplitude
halfPower <- uniroot(function(P) splineResponse(P, 32) - 1 / sqrt(2),
                     interval = c(33, 200))$root
round(halfPower, 1)
```

So a 32-year spline passes 71% of the amplitude at about `r round(halfPower)` years. Someone who reads "32-year cutoff" with signal-processing habits would put it a few years off.

The third is how gently it rolls off. On the response figure, the spline goes from keeping almost nothing to keeping almost everything over a range of several decades. A Butterworth filter makes the same change much more steeply, as [Smoothing and Filtering](14SmoothingFiltering.qmd) shows. Cook thought the broad transition was probably fine, given how uncertain the right smoothness is in the first place [@Cook1990, p. 112].

The fourth is the ends. The formula describes the spline in the middle of a long series. Near the ends it has data on one side only, and it behaves differently. Here is a 50-year cycle, 200 years long, through a 32-year spline.

```{r}
#| label: flt-ends
#| fig-cap: "A 50-year cycle (gray) through a 32-year spline (black). In the middle the spline carries most of the swing at a steady size. At the ends it bends toward the data."
endYears <- 1:200
endWave <- cos(2 * pi * endYears / 50)
endSpline <- caps(endWave, nyrs = 32)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(x = endYears, y = endWave), colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(aes(x = endYears, y = endSpline)) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: flt-ends-values
#| include: false
keepMiddle <- splineResponse(50, 32)
firstTen <- 1:10
peakSpline <- max(endSpline[firstTen])
peakWave <- max(endWave[firstTen])
```

In the middle, the spline keeps `r round(keepMiddle, 2)` of the cycle's amplitude, as the formula says. In the first ten years it peaks at `r round(peakSpline, 2)`, higher than the cycle itself gets in those years (`r round(peakWave, 2)`). The spline is a different filter at the ends. That matters most in the years you probably care about most, the recent end of a chronology. [Signal-Free](13SignalFree.qmd) and the section on the ends in [Smoothing and Filtering](14SmoothingFiltering.qmd) come back to it.

The last is division. Detrending divides each series by its curve instead of subtracting it, so the index is close to the high-pass side when the index is near 1 and drifts from it when the curve is small. [Detrending](09Detrending.qmd) looks at when that goes wrong.

None of that is a reason to drop the spline. You can set it in terms people care about, how long a wiggle to keep. It fits almost any growth curve without going wild. And decades of chronologies were built with it, so knowing exactly what it does is worth a lot.

## Back to the Book

The next filter you'll meet is the 32-year spline followed by prewhitening, in [Crossdating](06Crossdating.qmd), working on the fast side. When a later chapter says a spline of some number of years, this is the definition it means.
